title: The That's-Not-All Technique
description: Adding a bonus before the person can respond makes an offer feel more generous than it is.

sections.title: Quick Understanding
sections.content: The offer is made, then improved before the listener replies — "and if you order now, you also get…". The improvement feels like a concession, so the deal appears more valuable than the same package presented all at once.

sections.title: Why It Works
sections.content: The mind anchors on the first offer and treats the addition as a gain. Presented in one go, the identical package is just the price; presented in two steps, it feels like winning something extra.

sections.title: Real-Life Examples
content: A television shopping host adding free accessories after stating the price.
A market stallholder throwing in an extra item after you show interest.

sections.title: What It Looks Like
content: The price stated, then the sweetener added.
An unexpected bonus arriving before you can say no.

sections.title: Ethical Uses
sections.content: Adding a genuine extra to a fair offer is straightforward selling.

sections.title: Manipulative Uses
sections.content: Inflating the perceived value of an ordinary package with an "extra" that was always included.

sections.title: Red Flags
content: A bonus that appears only after you hesitate.
A price that could simply have been stated once.

sections.title: Defense Strategies
content: Judge the final package on its own merits, not as an improvement on the first version.
Ask what the offer would look like stated plainly.

sections.title: Mistakes People Make
content: Feeling that a bonus has been earned when it was built in.
Comparing the improved offer to the first offer instead of to the market.

sections.title: Key Lessons
content: Value the whole package, not the improvement.
